warmup.q: A Semaphore starts with 5 permits. One thread calls release() without ever calling acquire(). What does availablePermits() return?
warmup.why: Permits belong to nobody. A semaphore is a counter, and release() adds one whoever calls it. That's handy (one thread can acquire, another release), and it's also how a bug quietly raises your connection limit from 5 to 6, then 7. A lock would throw here; a semaphore can't.

sections.h: CountDownLatch waits for N events, once
sections.html:
A service that takes traffic before its caches are warm sends its first requests straight to Oracle. So the thread that opens the port has to wait until three loaders are done. join() from lesson 2 of this track can't do it if the loaders run on pool threads, because a pool thread doesn't end when its task does.

A CountDownLatch starts at a count. Any thread can call countDown(). Threads that call await() wait until the count reaches zero, then all of them go on. You used two of them in lesson 3 of this track to make threads collide.

Java
CountDownLatch warmedUp = new CountDownLatch(3);

// each warm-up thread, when it is done (in a finally):
warmedUp.countDown();

// the thread that opens the service for traffic:
if (!warmedUp.await(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
    throw new IllegalStateException("caches not warm after 30 s");
}
Kotlin
val warmedUp = CountDownLatch(3)

// each warm-up thread, when it is done (in a finally):
warmedUp.countDown()

// the thread that opens the service for traffic:
if (!warmedUp.await(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
    throw IllegalStateException("caches not warm after 30 s")
}

The latch waits for events, not for particular threads. One thread may count down three times, or three threads once each. It doesn't care.

It is also one-shot. Inside, the count is one atomic int. countDown() lowers it with a compare-and-set, the call that takes it to zero wakes every waiting thread, and no method ever raises it again. So once the count reaches zero, it stays there. Every later await() returns at once, and extra countDown() calls do nothing. There is no reset. If you need the same gate every round, you want a barrier, the next section.

Two habits keep latches from hanging services. Call countDown() in a finally, so a task that throws still counts. Otherwise the count never reaches zero and the waiter waits forever, WAITING in CountDownLatch.await in every thread dump. And prefer await(timeout, unit), which returns false if time ran out, so the caller can fail with a clear message instead of hanging.

A latch also carries visibility: everything a thread did before countDown() happens-before await() returns in the waiting thread. That is why the caller can read the warm-up results without another lock.

try.title: Open for traffic when the caches are warm
steps: Read LatchDemo. Three threads load three caches (200, 400 and 300 ms) and count down. main waits at most 2 seconds.
Predict when ready is printed, and what an extra countDown() does after that.
Run it, then run it again with -Pargs=stuck, where one load takes a minute.

code.title: LatchDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l10; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** * A service warms three caches in parallel and opens for traffic when all three are loaded. * Run with -Pargs=stuck to make one warm-up hang. */ public class LatchDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean stuck = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("stuck"); String[] caches = {"bin-ranges", "fx-rates", "merchant-config"}; long[] loadMs = {200, 400, stuck ? 60_000 : 300}; CountDownLatch warmedUp = new CountDownLatch(caches.length); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < caches.length; i++) { String name = caches[i]; long ms = loadMs[i]; Thread t = new Thread(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(ms); // pretend to load System.out.printf("%5d ms %s loaded%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, name); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } finally { warmedUp.countDown(); // count down even if loading failed } }, "warm-" + name); t.setDaemon(true); t.start(); } boolean ready = warmedUp.await(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // never wait forever at startup System.out.printf("%5d ms ready=%s, count=%d%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, ready, warmedUp.getCount()); // a latch is one-shot: once at zero, await() returns at once, forever if (ready) { warmedUp.countDown(); System.out.println("after another countDown(): count=" + warmedUp.getCount() + ", await returns at once: " + warmedUp.await(0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)); } } }

alt.title: LatchDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l10 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A service warms three caches in parallel and opens for traffic when all three are loaded. // Run with -Pargs=stuck to make one warm-up hang. fun main(args: Array<String>) { val stuck = args.firstOrNull() == "stuck" val caches = listOf("bin-ranges" to 200L, "fx-rates" to 400L, "merchant-config" to if (stuck) 60_000L else 300L) val warmedUp = CountDownLatch(caches.size) val t0 = System.nanoTime() for ((name, ms) in caches) { thread(isDaemon = true, name = "warm-$name") { try { Thread.sleep(ms) // pretend to load println("%5d ms %s loaded".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, name)) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } finally { warmedUp.countDown() // count down even if loading failed } } } val ready = warmedUp.await(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // never wait forever at startup println("%5d ms ready=%s, count=%d".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, ready, warmedUp.count)) // a latch is one-shot: once at zero, await() returns at once, forever if (ready) { warmedUp.countDown() println("after another countDown(): count=${warmedUp.count}, await returns at once: ${warmedUp.await(0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)}") } }

try.expect: The caches load at about 200, 300 and 400 ms, and ready=true, count=0 follows right after the slowest one. The extra countDown() leaves the count at 0, and await returns at once. With stuck, main prints ready=false, count=1 after 2 seconds instead of hanging forever.

sections.h: CyclicBarrier makes N threads meet, then all go on together
sections.html:
A CyclicBarrier waits for threads, not events. You give it a number of parties. Each thread calls await() when it reaches the meeting point and waits there until the last party arrives. Then all of them are released together, and the barrier resets itself for the next round. That is the cyclic part.

Java
CyclicBarrier endOfDay = new CyclicBarrier(4, () -> recordExposure(sum(shares)));   // the barrier action

// each of the 4 workers, for every simulated day:
shares[me] = simulate(me, day);
endOfDay.await();          // the 4th to arrive runs the action, then all 4 go on
Kotlin
val endOfDay = CyclicBarrier(4) { recordExposure(shares.sum()) }   // the barrier action

// each of the 4 workers, for every simulated day:
shares[me] = simulate(me, day)
endOfDay.await()          // the 4th to arrive runs the action, then all 4 go on

The optional barrier action runs once per round, on the last thread to arrive, before anyone is released. It's the place to combine results: each worker writes its own slot of shares before await(), and those writes are visible to the action and to every thread after the barrier. The figure shows two rounds.

A barrier can break. If a waiting thread is interrupted, or its await(timeout) times out, or the barrier action throws, the barrier is broken: the thread that timed out gets TimeoutException, and every other waiter, now and later, gets BrokenBarrierException until someone calls reset(). That is deliberate. A round with a missing party can't complete, and failing all of them is better than leaving the rest waiting forever.

But look at what doesn't break it: a thread that throws before it ever calls await(). The barrier can't know it's gone. The others wait, with plain await(), forever. So use the timed await in anything that runs in production.

Latch or barrier? A latch is a gate opened by events ("three caches loaded"). A barrier is a meeting point for a fixed group of threads ("all four workers finished day 3").

try.title: Three rounds, then a missing worker
steps: Read BarrierDemo. Three workers simulate three days; the barrier action prints the day's exposure and the name of the thread that ran it.
On day 4, worker 2 never arrives and the other two wait at most 300 ms. Predict what each of them prints.

code.title: BarrierDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l10; import java.util.concurrent.BrokenBarrierException; import java.util.concurrent.CyclicBarrier; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException; /** Three workers, three rounds, one barrier that resets itself. Then a round where one worker never shows up. */ public class BarrierDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { long[] shares = new long[3]; CyclicBarrier endOfDay = new CyclicBarrier(3, () -> // runs once per round, before anyone moves on System.out.printf(" day closed by %s: exposure %,d%n", Thread.currentThread().getName(), shares[0] + shares[1] + shares[2])); Thread[] workers = new Thread[3]; for (int w = 0; w < 3; w++) { int me = w; workers[w] = new Thread(() -> { try { for (int day = 1; day <= 3; day++) { Thread.sleep(50L * (me + 1)); // workers finish at different times shares[me] = 1_000L * day * (me + 1); endOfDay.await(); // wait for the other two } // day 4: worker 2 never arrives, the others give up after 300 ms if (me == 2) return; endOfDay.await(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); } catch (TimeoutException e) { System.out.println(" " + Thread.currentThread().getName() + ": TimeoutException, barrier now broken"); } catch (BrokenBarrierException e) { System.out.println(" " + Thread.currentThread().getName() + ": BrokenBarrierException"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, "worker-" + w); workers[w].start(); } for (Thread t : workers) t.join(); System.out.println("broken: " + endOfDay.isBroken()); } }

alt.title: BarrierDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l10 import java.util.concurrent.BrokenBarrierException import java.util.concurrent.CyclicBarrier import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Three workers, three rounds, one barrier that resets itself. Then a round where one worker never shows up. fun main() { val shares = LongArray(3) val endOfDay = CyclicBarrier(3) { // runs once per round, before anyone moves on println(" day closed by %s: exposure %,d".format(Thread.currentThread().name, shares.sum())) } val workers = List(3) { me -> thread(name = "worker-$me") { try { for (day in 1..3) { Thread.sleep(50L * (me + 1)) // workers finish at different times shares[me] = 1_000L * day * (me + 1) endOfDay.await() // wait for the other two } // day 4: worker 2 never arrives, the others give up after 300 ms if (me != 2) endOfDay.await(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) } catch (e: TimeoutException) { println(" ${Thread.currentThread().name}: TimeoutException, barrier now broken") } catch (e: BrokenBarrierException) { println(" ${Thread.currentThread().name}: BrokenBarrierException") } } } workers.forEach { it.join() } println("broken: ${endOfDay.isBroken}") }

try.expect: Three lines day closed by worker-2, with exposures 6,000, 12,000 and 18,000: worker 2 is the slowest, so it is always the last to arrive and runs the action. On day 4, one worker gets TimeoutException and breaks the barrier, and the other gets BrokenBarrierException. Which one gets which can change between runs. broken: true at the end.

sections.h: Semaphore limits how many threads do something at once
sections.html:
A Semaphore holds a number of permits. acquire() takes one, waiting while none are left. release() gives one back. With 20 permits, at most 20 threads can be between the two calls.

Java
private final Semaphore issuerPermits = new Semaphore(20);

Authorization authorize(Request r) throws InterruptedException {
    issuerPermits.acquire();             // before the try, like lock()
    try {
        return issuer.authorize(r);      // at most 20 threads in here
    } finally {
        issuerPermits.release();
    }
}
Kotlin
private val issuerPermits = Semaphore(20)

fun authorize(r: Request): Authorization {
    issuerPermits.acquire()              // before the try, like lock()
    try {
        return issuer.authorize(r)       // at most 20 threads in here
    } finally {
        issuerPermits.release()
    }
}

This is how you protect something that tolerates N users but not N + 1: a card-issuer API that throttles above 20 concurrent calls per client, a pool of 20 database connections, a CPU-heavy PDF renderer. tryAcquire(timeout, unit) waits a bounded time and returns false if no permit came free, so a request can fail fast instead of piling up.

The idiom is the one from explicit locks: acquire() before the try, release() in finally. It matters even more here, because of the property from the warm-up: permits have no owner. A lock knows who holds it and throws if a stranger releases it. A semaphore is just a counter. Both of these bugs silently raise your limit:

  • calling acquire() inside the try, so an interrupted wait still runs the release() in finally;
  • ignoring the result of tryAcquire, then running the task and releasing anyway.

The lab's IssuerGate has both. Every extra release is a permanent extra permit, and a limit of 20 drifts to 30 over a day of interrupts and timeouts. No exception, no log line.

Two more points. A Semaphore limits one JVM: six pods with 20 permits each send up to 120 calls to the issuer, so divide the issuer's limit by your pod count. And new Semaphore(20, true) makes it fair, which stops a fast thread from grabbing permits ahead of threads that have waited longer.

try.title: Five permits, twenty calls
steps: Read SemaphoreDemo. Twenty threads each make a 100 ms issuer call through a Semaphore(5), and the demo tracks the peak number in flight.
Predict the peak and the total time.
Run it. Then move issuer.acquire() to inside the try in the Java version: does anything change in this run? Why might it in production?

code.title: SemaphoreDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l10; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** 20 authorizations, 5 issuer permits, 100 ms per call. Then the bug that adds permits out of thin air. */ public class SemaphoreDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Semaphore issuer = new Semaphore(5); AtomicInteger inFlight = new AtomicInteger(), peak = new AtomicInteger(); Thread[] requests = new Thread[20]; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < requests.length; i++) { requests[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { issuer.acquire(); // before the try try { peak.accumulateAndGet(inFlight.incrementAndGet(), Math::max); Thread.sleep(100); // the call to the issuer inFlight.decrementAndGet(); } finally { issuer.release(); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); requests[i].start(); } for (Thread t : requests) t.join(); System.out.printf("20 calls, peak in flight %d, took %d ms%n", peak.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); // permits belong to nobody: any thread can release, even one that never acquired Semaphore pool = new Semaphore(5); pool.release(); System.out.println("new Semaphore(5), then one stray release(): " + pool.availablePermits() + " permits"); } }

alt.title: SemaphoreDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l10 import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread // 20 authorizations, 5 issuer permits, 100 ms per call. Then the bug that adds permits out of thin air. private inline fun <T> Semaphore.withPermit(block: () -> T): T { acquire() // before the try try { return block() } finally { release() } } fun main() { val issuer = Semaphore(5) val inFlight = AtomicInteger() val peak = AtomicInteger() val t0 = System.nanoTime() val requests = List(20) { thread { issuer.withPermit { peak.accumulateAndGet(inFlight.incrementAndGet(), Math::max) Thread.sleep(100) // the call to the issuer inFlight.decrementAndGet() } } } requests.forEach { it.join() } println("20 calls, peak in flight ${peak.get()}, took ${(System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000} ms") // permits belong to nobody: any thread can release, even one that never acquired val pool = Semaphore(5) pool.release() println("new Semaphore(5), then one stray release(): ${pool.availablePermits()} permits") }

try.expect: Peak in flight 5, total about 400 ms: four waves of five calls. The stray release() turns 5 permits into 6. Moving acquire() inside the try changes nothing here, because nobody interrupts the waiters. In production an interrupt during the wait (a cancelled request, a shutdown) would release a permit that was never taken.

sections.html:
A Phaser is a barrier whose group can change size. Parties register() to join and arriveAndDeregister() to leave, and each phase waits only for the parties registered at that moment. Phases are numbered from 0, and you can override onAdvance(phase, parties) to run code between phases and to end the phaser by returning true.

Java
Phaser phaser = new Phaser(1);          // the coordinator is a party
phaser.register();                      // each worker joins when it starts
phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance();         // wait for everyone still registered
phaser.arriveAndDeregister();           // leave; later phases wait for one party fewer
Kotlin
val phaser = Phaser(1)          // the coordinator is a party
phaser.register()               // each worker joins when it starts
phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance()  // wait for everyone still registered
phaser.arriveAndDeregister()    // leave; later phases wait for one party fewer

Use it when the number of workers isn't known up front or changes between phases: a settlement run where some workers only fetch and then leave, or a job that registers one party per file it discovers. If the group is fixed, a CyclicBarrier is simpler and says what it means. A phaser can also replace a CountDownLatch that you'd like to reuse.

An Exchanger is the smallest synchronizer: two threads meet and swap one object each, for example a full buffer for an empty one. You will rarely need it.

CountDownLatch and Semaphore are built on AbstractQueuedSynchronizer, like ReentrantLock. CyclicBarrier uses a ReentrantLock and a Condition inside, and Phaser and Exchanger park their threads with LockSupport directly. So a thread waiting in any of them is parked and shows as WAITING or TIMED_WAITING in a thread dump, with the synchronizer's class in its stack. And none of them has an owner the deadlock detector can see, so a cycle of threads waiting on semaphores or latches is never reported as a deadlock.

try.title: A worker leaves halfway
steps: Read PhaserDemo. Three workers run three phases (fetch, net, post). Worker 2 leaves after the first phase. onAdvance prints each phase and the parties left.
Predict the party count printed for each phase.

code.title: PhaserDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l10; import java.util.concurrent.Phaser; /** A settlement run in three phases. One worker leaves after the first phase; the Phaser just has fewer parties. */ public class PhaserDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { String[] phases = {"fetch", "net", "post"}; Phaser phaser = new Phaser(1) { // 1 party: main, until it deregisters @Override protected boolean onAdvance(int phase, int parties) { System.out.printf(" phase %d (%s) done, %d parties%n", phase, phases[phase], parties); return phase == phases.length - 1 || parties == 0; // true ends the phaser } }; Thread[] workers = new Thread[3]; for (int w = 0; w < workers.length; w++) { int me = w; phaser.register(); // a new party joins workers[w] = new Thread(() -> { for (int p = 0; p < phases.length; p++) { if (me == 2 && p == 1) { phaser.arriveAndDeregister(); // worker 2 only fetches, then leaves return; } phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance(); // like a barrier, for this phase } }); workers[w].start(); } phaser.arriveAndDeregister(); // main stops taking part for (Thread t : workers) t.join(); System.out.println("terminated: " + phaser.isTerminated()); } }

alt.title: PhaserDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l10 import java.util.concurrent.Phaser import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A settlement run in three phases. One worker leaves after the first phase; the Phaser just has fewer parties. fun main() { val phases = listOf("fetch", "net", "post") val phaser = object : Phaser(1) { // 1 party: main, until it deregisters override fun onAdvance(phase: Int, parties: Int): Boolean { println(" phase %d (%s) done, %d parties".format(phase, phases[phase], parties)) return phase == phases.lastIndex || parties == 0 // true ends the phaser } } val workers = List(3) { me -> phaser.register() // a new party joins thread(start = true) { for (p in phases.indices) { if (me == 2 && p == 1) { phaser.arriveAndDeregister() // worker 2 only fetches, then leaves return@thread } phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance() // like a barrier, for this phase } } } phaser.arriveAndDeregister() // main stops taking part workers.forEach { it.join() } println("terminated: ${phaser.isTerminated}") }

try.expect: phase 0 (fetch) done, 3 parties, then phase 1 (net) done, 2 parties and phase 2 (post) done, 2 parties, then terminated: true. main registered itself first so no phase could finish before every worker had joined, then left. Worker 2's arriveAndDeregister counts as its arrival for phase 1 and shrinks every later phase.

analogy: A CountDownLatch is a rocket countdown: when it reaches zero the launch happens, and you can't count down again. A CyclicBarrier is a tour group regrouping at every landmark: the bus leaves only when everyone is back, and the guide (the barrier action) does a head count each time. A Semaphore is a car park with 20 spaces and a sign showing how many are free; nobody checks which car leaves, so a car that never parked can still "leave" and the sign shows 21. A Phaser is a relay race where runners can join or drop out between legs. The analogy breaks at the tour bus: a guide would go looking for a missing tourist. A barrier just waits, forever, unless you gave await a timeout.
world: In a Quarkus service, a latch shows up at startup (open for traffic after the BIN ranges and FX rates load) and in almost every concurrency test you write. A semaphore shows up in front of anything with a concurrency limit: a card-issuer API that throttles at 20 calls per client, a PDF generator, a Temporal activity that calls a partner with a strict rate limit. Remember the multiplication: the limit is per JVM, so 6 pods with 20 permits each is 120 calls at the partner. Barriers and phasers are rarer in request-handling code and common in batch jobs: an end-of-day exposure simulation or a reconciliation that runs in phases across worker threads.
mistake: The most common real mistake is releasing a permit you never acquired. It happens in two ways: acquire() placed inside the try, so an interrupted wait still reaches the release() in finally, and tryAcquire(timeout) whose false result is ignored. Both look fine in review and in tests, because tests rarely interrupt waiters or exhaust permits. In production, each cancelled request or timeout adds one permit for good, and the limit that protected the issuer API slowly stops limiting. The fix is the lock idiom: acquire() on the line before try, and if (!tryAcquire(...)) that returns or throws before the try is entered.

compare.title: A permit helper in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java
java.html: static <T> T withPermit(Semaphore s, Callable<T> task) throws Exception { s.acquire(); // before the try, like lock() try { return task.call(); } finally { s.release(); // exactly the permit we took } } Authorization a = withPermit(issuerPermits, () -> issuer.authorize(request));

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.html: inline fun <T> Semaphore.withPermit(block: () -> T): T { acquire() // before the try, like lock() try { return block() } finally { release() // exactly the permit we took } } val a = issuerPermits.withPermit { issuer.authorize(request) }

compare.note: Both languages use the same java.util.concurrent classes, and both block a thread while it waits. Kotlin's difference is that an inline extension function makes the safe idiom read like a language feature: the lambda is inlined, so there's no allocation, return inside it works as usual, and nobody on the team writes the try/finally by hand again. The Kotlin standard library doesn't ship withPermit for java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; you write it once, as above. kotlinx.coroutines has its own Semaphore with a built-in withPermit that suspends the coroutine instead of blocking a thread. The coroutines track covers it.

worked.title: A parallel reconciliation that can't hang

steps.say: End-of-day reconciliation compares 4 ledger partitions against the bank statement. Each takes a few seconds, so it runs on 4 threads and waits for all of them with a latch. Read this first version. What happens if reconcile throws for one partition?
steps.code: CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(4); List<Mismatch> found = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); for (Partition p : partitions) { new Thread(() -> { found.addAll(reconcile(p)); done.countDown(); }).start(); } done.await(); report(found);

alt.html: val done = CountDownLatch(4) val found = CopyOnWriteArrayList<Mismatch>() for (p in partitions) { thread { found.addAll(reconcile(p)) done.countDown() } } done.await() report(found)

steps.say: The failing thread dies before countDown(). The count stays at 1, and await() waits forever. The job doesn't fail; it just never ends. A dump shows main WAITING in CountDownLatch.await and no worker threads at all, because they all finished or died. The fix has three parts: count down in finally, record the failure so it isn't lost, and never wait without a deadline.
Here is the version that always ends, with subgoal labels.
steps.code: CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(partitions.size()); List<Mismatch> found = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); List<Throwable> failures = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); for (Partition p : partitions) { new Thread(() -> { try { found.addAll(reconcile(p)); // 1. do the work } catch (Throwable e) { failures.add(e); // 2. remember the failure instead of losing it } finally { done.countDown(); // 3. always count down } }, "recon-" + p.id()).start(); } if (!done.await(10, TimeUnit.MINUTES)) { // 4. never wait forever throw new IllegalStateException("reconciliation still running after 10 min"); } if (!failures.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalStateException("partitions failed: " + failures); report(found); // 5. countDown happens-before await returns: all results visible

alt.html: val done = CountDownLatch(partitions.size) val found = CopyOnWriteArrayList<Mismatch>() val failures = CopyOnWriteArrayList<Throwable>() for (p in partitions) { thread(name = "recon-${p.id}") { try { found.addAll(reconcile(p)) // 1. do the work } catch (e: Throwable) { failures.add(e) // 2. remember the failure instead of losing it } finally { done.countDown() // 3. always count down } } } if (!done.await(10, TimeUnit.MINUTES)) { // 4. never wait forever throw IllegalStateException("reconciliation still running after 10 min") } if (failures.isNotEmpty()) throw IllegalStateException("partitions failed: $failures") report(found) // 5. countDown happens-before await returns: all results visible

steps.say: Before reading on, explain to yourself: why can main read found after await returns without any lock? Answer: everything a worker did before countDown() happens-before await() returns in the thread that waited. found is still a CopyOnWriteArrayList, because the four workers add to it at the same time. In a real service you'd submit the four tasks to an ExecutorService and use invokeAll, which the executors track covers. A latch is one of the pieces such tools are built from.

lab.title: Fix a permit leak, then run a simulation in rounds
steps: Run the tests. Four of six fail: the timed call runs its task with no permit, an interrupted waiter adds a permit, and both RoundRunner tests hit UnsupportedOperationException.
Fix IssuerGate.call(task): move acquire() to the line before the try.
Fix IssuerGate.call(task, maxWait): if tryAcquire returns false, throw TimeoutException before the try, so the task doesn't run and nothing is released.

Write RoundRunner.run. Keep a long[] shares, one slot per worker. Build a CyclicBarrier(workers, action) whose action sums shares and calls onRoundTotal. Start one thread per worker that loops over the rounds: shares[me] = step.applyAsLong(me, r), then await(). Join every thread before returning.
Run the tests until all six pass, then twice more.
hints: Why can the barrier action read shares without a lock? Each worker writes only its own slot, before await(), and everything before await() happens-before the action runs.
await() throws InterruptedException and BrokenBarrierException. In the worker, restore the interrupt flag for the first, and stop the loop for both.

The second RoundRunner test calls your step from 4 threads and checks that round r never starts before r totals have been passed on. The barrier action runs before anyone is released, so this holds by construction.
lab.done: All six tests in SynchronizersTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Wait for N tasks, with a deadline
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write awaitAll(tasks, deadline): run each task on its own thread and return true if all of them finished within the deadline, false otherwise. A task that throws must not make it hang. Check: where is your countDown()?

answer.html: static boolean awaitAll(List<Runnable> tasks, Duration deadline) throws InterruptedException { CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(tasks.size()); for (Runnable task : tasks) { new Thread(() -> { try { task.run(); } finally { done.countDown(); // even when the task throws } }).start(); } return done.await(deadline.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: fun awaitAll(tasks: List<() -> Unit>, deadline: Duration): Boolean { val done = CountDownLatch(tasks.size) for (task in tasks) { thread { try { task() } finally { done.countDown() // even when the task throws } } } return done.await(deadline.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) }

recap: CountDownLatch: wait until N events have happened. One-shot; count down in finally; await with a timeout.
CyclicBarrier: N threads meet, the barrier action runs once on the last arrival, then all continue. It resets itself each round and breaks on timeout or interrupt.
A thread that never reaches await() leaves the others waiting forever unless they use the timed await.
Semaphore: at most N threads at once. Permits have no owner, so release only what you acquired: acquire() before try, check tryAcquire's result.
Phaser: a reusable barrier whose parties can register and leave between phases. Exchanger swaps one object between two threads.
Releasing a latch, barrier or semaphore happens-before the waiting threads continue, so results written before it are visible after it.

explain.prompt: Explain the difference between a CountDownLatch, a CyclicBarrier and a Semaphore to a teammate, with one payments example of each.
explain.answer: A latch waits for a number of events and then opens for good: startup code waits until the BIN ranges, FX rates and merchant config have loaded, then starts taking traffic. A barrier is a meeting point for a fixed group of threads, every round: four workers simulating exposure each finish day 3, the last one totals the day, and then all four start day 4. A semaphore limits how many threads do something at the same time: at most 20 threads may be inside a call to the card issuer. The traps differ too. A latch hangs if a task forgets to count down. A barrier hangs if a thread never arrives and nobody used a timeout. A semaphore quietly raises its limit if code releases a permit it never took.

deeper.html:
CountDownLatch and Semaphore, like ReentrantLock, are thin layers over AbstractQueuedSynchronizer: an int of state and a queue of parked threads. For a latch the state is the count, and await parks until it is zero. For a semaphore it is the permits left. CyclicBarrier is a ReentrantLock with one Condition, and Phaser and Exchanger keep their own queues of parked threads. All of them park through LockSupport, which is why they show up the same way in a thread dump: WAITING (parking), with a line like parking to wait for <0x...> (a java.util.concurrent.Semaphore$NonfairSync).

A few API corners are worth knowing. Semaphore.acquire(n) takes several permits in one step, which avoids the hold-one-wait-for-another deadlock from the quiz. drainPermits() takes all that are left, which is handy when you want to stop new work during a shutdown. acquireUninterruptibly() ignores interrupts, which you almost never want. CyclicBarrier.await() returns the arrival index (parties minus one for the first to arrive, zero for the last), so you can pick one thread to do extra work without a barrier action.

Phaser supports tiering: you can build a tree of phasers so thousands of parties don't all contend on one. Its Javadoc caps a single phaser at 65,535 registered parties.

On virtual threads (JDK 21), blocking in any of these is cheap: the virtual thread parks and its carrier thread runs something else. A Semaphore is in fact the standard way to limit concurrency once you start a virtual thread per task, because there is no pool size to do it for you. The virtual threads track comes back to that. In Kotlin coroutines, the equivalents suspend instead of blocking: kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore, Job.join() or awaitAll() for latches, and channels for most of the rest.
